_meta.descricao: Catechetical path of preparation for First Communion, mirroring the one that already exists for Confirmation: the sacrament, the Mass, confession, and the Eucharistic life.
_meta.aviso: Initial set of catechetical topics; it does not replace a catechism or a complete parish preparation program for the sacraments.
fontes_gerais: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1322-1419

itens.resumo: What the Eucharist is: a sacrament of Christian initiation in which Jesus becomes present under the species of bread and wine.
itens.corpo:
The Eucharist is, together with Baptism and Confirmation, the third sacrament of Christian initiation, and the Catechism calls it "the source and summit of the Christian life" (CCC 1324): in it is contained the whole spiritual good of the Church, namely Christ himself. At the Last Supper, on the night before he died, Jesus took bread and wine, gave thanks, broke the bread and said "This is my body" and "This is the cup of my blood", commanding the apostles to do the same in memory of him.

First Communion is the moment when the child, already baptized and duly prepared through catechesis, receives for the first time the Body of Christ under the species of consecrated bread.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1324

itens.resumo: On the eve of his death, Jesus institutes the Eucharist during the Jewish Passover meal with the apostles.
itens.corpo: On the night before he suffered, Jesus gathered with the Twelve to celebrate the Jewish Passover meal, which recalled the liberation from Egypt. During this meal, he instituted a new and definitive memorial: he took the bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying "Take, eat; this is my Body"; then he took the cup of wine and said "Drink of it, all of you; for this is my Blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Mt 26:26-28). At the end, he commanded: "Do this in memory of me" (Lk 22:19) — a mandate that the Church fulfills at every Mass to this day.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1337-1340

itens.resumo: The Catholic faith that, after the consecration, the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ.
itens.corpo: The Church teaches that, by the words of consecration spoken by the priest at Mass, the bread and wine are substantially converted into the Body and Blood of Christ, with only the appearances (color, taste, texture) of bread and wine remaining — what theology calls "transubstantiation." It is not a symbol, nor merely a spiritual remembrance: it is Christ himself, true God and true man, present in a real, true, and substantial way under the Eucharistic species, and this presence remains as long as the consecrated species subsist — which is why the Blessed Sacrament is kept in the tabernacle and adored outside of Mass.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1373-1377

itens.resumo: Knowing the structure of the Mass helps the child participate attentively and understand what is happening at the altar.
itens.corpo: The Mass has two great parts, united in a single act of worship: the Liturgy of the Word, in which the biblical readings and the Gospel are proclaimed, followed by the homily; and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, in which the bread and wine are prepared and presented, the priest consecrates them in the Eucharistic Prayer, and the faithful are united with Christ in communion. Around these two central parts, the introductory rites (greeting, penitential act, Gloria) prepare the heart, and the concluding rites (blessing, dismissal) send the faithful forth to live what they have celebrated. Understanding this structure helps the child follow the Mass attentively, not merely as a passive spectator.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1348-1355

itens.resumo: The period of specific catechesis that precedes First Communion, deepening faith and understanding of the sacrament.
itens.corpo: Preparation for First Communion is a specific catechetical time, usually lasting one or two years, in which the child deepens his or her knowledge of the Catholic faith — the Trinity, the life of Jesus, the commandments, prayer — with special attention to the Eucharistic mystery that he or she is about to receive. Unlike a simple school lesson, this preparation also seeks to form habits of prayer, participation in Sunday Mass, and the practice of charity, ideally involving the whole family in accompanying the child and in the witness of Christian life at home.
itens.imagem_credito: Schweig, Aimee Mae Goldstone, 1897-1987 — Wikimedia Commons, No restrictions
fontes: General Directory for Catechesis

itens.resumo: Before First Communion, the child is prepared to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation for the first time.
itens.corpo: It is a traditional and recommended practice of the Church that the child receive the sacrament of Confession (Reconciliation) for the first time shortly before his or her First Communion, usually during the same stage of catechetical preparation. This allows the child to approach the Eucharist in a state of grace, understanding from an early age that the two sacraments go together: Confession purifies and reconciles, the Eucharist nourishes and strengthens. The child is prepared to make a simple examination of conscience, suited to his or her age, and to understand confession as an encounter with mercy, not as a feared interrogation.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1422-1424

itens.resumo: Abstaining from food and drink for a brief period before Communion, a sign of desire and spiritual preparation.
itens.corpo: The Church asks the faithful to observe a brief Eucharistic fast, now reduced to just one hour before receiving Communion, not counting water and medicine, as a sign of respect and of spiritual desire for the sacrament they are about to receive. Historically stricter (even requiring a fast from the previous midnight), the fast was gradually relaxed over the course of the twentieth century to make frequent Communion easier, but it remained as a small ascetic gesture that helps prepare the body and spirit for the encounter with Christ.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1387
Code of Canon Law, can. 919

itens.resumo: Wheat bread and grape wine are the essential matter of the sacrament, changed into the Body and Blood of Christ; the Latin Church uses unleavened bread, and the Eastern rites use leavened bread.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism defines the matter of the sacrament in no. 1412: "the essential signs of the Eucharistic sacrament are wheat bread and grape wine", upon which the blessing of the Holy Spirit is invoked and the words of consecration spoken by Jesus at the Last Supper are pronounced. Unleavened bread is therefore not required as a condition of validity: the Church recognizes as valid the consecration of both unleavened and leavened bread. This is a question of liturgical discipline, not of the essence of the sacrament. The Catechism itself observes (no. 1413) that by the consecration transubstantiation takes place: under the species of bread and wine, Christ, living and glorious, is present in a true, real, and substantial manner.

The word "host" comes from the Latin hostia, which designated the victim or offering immolated in sacrifice. Applied to the Eucharist, it evokes Christ's self-offering as an innocent victim on the cross, sacramentally renewed. Before the consecration, the unleavened bread is technically called a particle; only after it is consecrated is it properly called a host. The other element is the wine of the vine, pure and not spoiled.

The use of unleavened bread in the West has its roots in the Jewish Passover meal, in which leaven was not permitted. It became a widespread practice in the Latin rite from the ninth century onward and was later fixed as a disciplinary obligation. The Churches of Eastern tradition, on the other hand, maintained the use of leavened bread (the prosphora). This difference in custom, together with the Filioque, the question of Roman primacy, and the observance of the Sabbaths, fueled the so-called Azymite controversy, which preceded the East-West Schism. Around 1053, Archbishop Leo of Ohrid addressed a letter to Bishop John of Trani criticizing the Latins precisely for their use of unleavened bread; the Patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, supported the accusations, and the papal legate, Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, responded on behalf of Pope Saint Leo IX. In 1054, the mutual excommunication between Humbert and Cerularius marked the rupture. It is, therefore, a material detail whose historical and ecumenical weight was enormous.

In the Roman stational churches of antiquity, the faithful brought bread and wine for the offering; from the ninth century onward, the clergy began to prepare the hosts separately, with special care, and the custom of offerings by the people gradually disappeared. Since then the Eucharistic bread usually bears engraved signs that distinguish it from ordinary bread. The preparation of the particles and the provenance of the wine thus became objects of the Church's disciplinary attention, so that the mystery may rest on worthy matter: simple bread and wine, chosen by Christ, which become the vehicle of the greatest of the sacraments.

itens.resumo: The gestures of respect — reverence before receiving, hands that welcome the host, silence — that accompany the reception of Communion, and the liturgical norms that regulate them.
itens.corpo:
The reception of Communion is surrounded, in the Catholic tradition, by concrete signs of reverence before the real presence of Christ. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal (GIRM) describes the moment (no. 161): if Communion is distributed under the species of bread alone, the priest raises the host slightly and shows it to each communicant, saying "The Body of Christ"; the faithful respond "Amen" and receive the Sacrament on the tongue or, where permitted, in the hand, as they prefer, consuming the host immediately and in its entirety. The response "Amen" is the act of faith that precedes the gesture.

Regarding posture and gesture, the instruction Redemptionis Sacramentum (2004), from the Congregation for Divine Worship, establishes in no. 90: the faithful receive Communion kneeling or standing, as determined by the Conference of Bishops with the confirmation of the Apostolic See; and, when they receive Communion standing, it is recommended that they make a due act of reverence before receiving the Sacrament — as a rule, a bow of the head before the Sacrament. This is not mere etiquette: the same document, in no. 91, forbids denying Communion to a member of the faithful solely because he or she wishes to receive it kneeling or standing.

The teaching balances strictness and freedom. Communion in the hand was widely reintroduced in the West after the Second Vatican Council, and the practice of receiving on the tongue has never ceased to be fully legitimate; the choice between the two belongs to the individual, according to the norms of the region itself. What the Church asks is that either form be accompanied by the awareness of standing before the Lord.

The concrete gestures — the bow or genuflection before receiving Communion, the hands joined or cupped to receive the host so that no fragment falls from it, the interior silence after Communion — help to form from an early age the sense that what is received there is not "a piece of bread" but Christ himself. For First Communion catechesis, teaching the child to make these gestures with care, without haste and without embarrassment is to teach him or her, in practice, what it means to believe in the real presence; the body that bows and the hands that open educate a faith that is still stammering.

itens.resumo: The spiritual effects that the reception of the Eucharist produces in those who receive it in a state of grace: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sins, preservation from grave sins, and the building up of the Church.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism of the Catholic Church gathers in seven paragraphs (1391-1397) the "fruits of Communion," and the first of them is intimate union with Christ. It cites the promise of Jesus himself in the discourse on the bread of life: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him" (Jn 6:56), and also "he who eats me will live because of me" (Jn 6:57). Communion is not merely devotion: it is the foundation of life in Christ itself.

The Catechism compares this effect to that of material food on the body (no. 1392): Communion "preserves, increases, and renews the life of grace received at Baptism." This bread of the pilgrimage is called viaticum when received shortly before death — the Latin word viaticum designates precisely the provision given to one setting out on a journey.

The third fruit is purification from sin (nos. 1393-1395). The Blood of Christ, "poured out for the forgiveness of sins," cannot unite us to Christ without at the same time cleansing us of past sins and preserving us from future ones. Here the Catechism cites Saint Ambrose in the work De sacramentis (4,28): "If whenever his blood is poured out, it is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, I should always receive it, so that it may always forgive my sins. If I always sin, I should always have a remedy." No. 1394 recalls the Council of Trent in teaching that the Eucharist strengthens the charity that tends to grow cold in daily life and, for this reason, wipes away venial sins; no. 1395 further specifies that the Eucharist preserves from future mortal sins, but "is not ordered to the forgiveness of mortal sins," which belongs to the sacrament of Reconciliation.

There is also an ecclesial fruit (no. 1396): "the Eucharist makes the Church." Alluding to 1 Cor 10:16-17 — "The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body" —, it teaches that Communion renews and deepens the incorporation into the Church already accomplished by Baptism. Ancient formulations of the tradition already called the Eucharist the "medicine of immortality": Saint Ignatius of Antioch, at the beginning of the second century, describes the Eucharistic bread as "the medicine of immortality, the antidote against death, enabling us to live forever in Jesus Christ" (Letter to the Ephesians 20:2).

Hence the recommendation of frequent reception (no. 1417): those who take part in Mass are earnestly urged to receive Communion, and the Church imposes on the faithful the duty of receiving Communion at least once a year, at Easter time. For First Communion catechumens, these fruits explain why the sacrament is not an isolated rite of a single day, but a source of Christian life to be nourished throughout the whole of one's existence.

itens.resumo: An act of fervent desire to receive Christ, practiced by those who cannot receive sacramental Communion at that moment.
itens.corpo: Spiritual communion is the ardent desire and interior supplication to receive Christ in the Eucharist, made by one who, for some reason, cannot receive sacramental Communion at that moment — because he is not present at Mass, because he is in grave sin with no immediate possibility of confession, or because of any other impediment. Saints such as Alphonsus Liguori recommended its frequent practice, teaching simple prayers to express this desire. Although it does not replace sacramental Communion when the latter is possible, it is recognized by the spiritual tradition as a real source of grace and union with Christ, though not identical to sacramental Communion.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1418

itens.resumo: The custom of dressing children in white for First Communion symbolizes purity and the joy of encountering Christ.
itens.corpo: It is an ancient and widespread tradition, especially since the nineteenth century, for boys and girls to dress in white on the day of their First Communion — a custom that recalls the symbolism of the white garment of Baptism, a sign of purity and of new life in Christ, and of the festive joy proper to a nuptial encounter with the Lord (an image dear to the biblical tradition of the wedding banquet). Although it is not a mandatory liturgical requirement and varies according to culture and era, the custom helps to mark visually, for the child and for the assembled community, the uniqueness and solemnity of that day.
itens.imagem_credito: Schweig, Aimee Mae Goldstone, 1897-1987 — Wikimedia Commons, No restrictions
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1243 (white garment of Baptism)

itens.titulo: The Role of the Family in Preparation
itens.resumo: Parents and godparents are the child's first catechists, and their example of Christian life is decisive during this period.
itens.corpo: Although formal catechesis is conducted by catechists in the parish, the Church insists that parents remain the "first and principal educators in the faith" of their children (CCC 2223), and their concrete witness of Christian life — participation in Sunday Mass, prayer at home, the practice of charity — weighs more in the child's spiritual formation than any isolated classroom instruction. Preparation for First Communion is, therefore, also an occasion for the family itself to rediscover or deepen its practice of the faith, closely accompanying the catechetical journey of their son or daughter.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 2223

itens.resumo: The Church asks only that the child have sufficient use of reason to distinguish the Eucharistic bread from ordinary bread before receiving Communion.
itens.corpo: The Code of Canon Law establishes that First Communion is to be received upon reaching the "age of discretion" (generally around seven years old), understood not as a rigorous academic examination, but as the minimum capacity of the child to understand, with faith proportionate to his or her age, that what he or she is about to receive is not ordinary bread, but the Body of Christ, worthy of love and adoration. Saint Pius X, at the beginning of the twentieth century, decisively lowered the age of First Communion, which had previously often been reserved for adolescence, precisely so as not to deprive young children of the spiritual nourishment of the Eucharist for an unnecessarily long time.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, can. 913
Saint Pius X, Decree Quam Singulari (1910)

itens.resumo: The encouragement, ordinary today, for the faithful to receive Communion at every Mass they attend, not only on special occasions.
itens.corpo: Until the early twentieth century, it was relatively common for the faithful to receive Communion only a few times a year, even when they took part in Mass regularly. In the decree "Sacra Tridentina Synodus" (1905), Saint Pius X strongly encouraged the practice of frequent and even daily Communion for all the faithful in a state of grace and with a right intention, reversing centuries of more infrequent practice motivated by excessive reverential fear. Today the Church recommends that the faithful receive Communion at every Mass they attend, provided they are in a state of grace, as the ordinary way of nourishing the spiritual life.
fontes: Saint Pius X, Decree Sacra Tridentina Synodus (1905)

itens.resumo: Praying before the exposed Blessed Sacrament, recognizing and adoring the real presence of Christ outside the celebration of Mass.
itens.corpo:
Besides being received in Communion, the Eucharist can be adored outside of Mass: the priest exposes the consecrated host in a vessel called a monstrance, and the faithful gather to pray before it in silence, recognizing there the real presence of Christ. This devotion developed above all from the Middle Ages onward, linked to the Eucharistic movement of the Abbey of Cornillon, in Belgium, which also gave rise to the feast of Corpus Christi in the thirteenth century.

A child preparing for First Communion can begin to become familiar with this form of prayer by visiting the church during times of adoration or by taking part in simple celebrations before the Blessed Sacrament, learning from an early age that the Communion received at Mass does not exhaust the presence of Christ: He remains truly present as long as the consecrated species subsist, and can be visited and adored at any moment.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1378-1379

itens.resumo: The place of honor in the church where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, marked by a small lamp that is always lit.
itens.corpo:
The tabernacle (from the Latin tabernaculum, "tent") is the place where the church keeps the consecrated hosts: originally, it served chiefly so that Communion could be brought to the sick and the absent outside of Mass. As faith in the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist deepened, the Church also came to value silent adoration of the Lord present there, and the tabernacle came to hold a place of prominence and dignity within the church building.

Beside the tabernacle a small lamp — usually red — burns continuously, a visible sign that the Blessed Sacrament is reserved there. Teaching the child to recognize this light and to genuflect when passing before the tabernacle is a simple and concrete way to form, from an early age, a sense of reverence before the real presence of Christ kept in the church even outside the hours of Mass.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1379

itens.titulo: Receiving Communion in the Hand or on the Tongue
itens.resumo: The two forms currently permitted for receiving the consecrated host, and the care and reverence that both require of the one receiving Communion.
itens.corpo:
The more traditional practice, and still the usual form in many places today, is to receive the host directly on the tongue. After the Second Vatican Council, however, the custom of receiving Communion in the hand spread in several countries. The Instruction Memoriale Domini, approved by Pope Saint Paul VI in 1969, acknowledged that this practice had already existed in very ancient times of Christianity, and that it could be authorized by episcopal conferences where it had already become an established custom, provided that the liturgical norms were respected and faith in the real presence was clearly preserved.

Whichever form is chosen—always according to the norm in force in the diocese—the essential thing is that the child understands that he or she is receiving the very Body of Christ, and not mere food: for this reason the Church asks, in both cases, for gestures of care and reverence, avoiding any carelessness with the consecrated particles.
fontes: Sacred Congregation for Divine Worship, Instruction Memoriale Domini (1969)

itens.resumo: Receiving both the bread and the chalice: an ancient practice, restricted for centuries to the bread alone, and today once again possible in certain celebrations.
itens.corpo:
In the first centuries of the Church, the faithful received Communion under both species — the consecrated bread and wine. From the end of the eleventh century, however, the custom began to spread of distributing the Eucharist to the faithful only under the form of bread, a practice that the Council of Constance made the general norm in 1415. The Council of Trent, later, taught that Christ is present "whole and entire" even under a single species, so that whoever receives only the bread already receives the Lord fully — body, blood, soul, and divinity.

In 1963, the conciliar constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium of the Second Vatican Council again authorized the distribution of Communion under both species in certain celebrations, understanding that the sign of the Eucharistic banquet is expressed more completely in this way. For this reason, today, on occasions such as the First Communion of a small group or specific celebrations, it is possible for the faithful to receive also from the chalice — always as an additional option, never as a replacement for Communion under the species of bread, which by itself is already complete.
fontes: Council of Trent, Doctrine on Communion under Both Kinds
Second Vatican Council, Constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1390

itens.resumo: Being baptized, in a state of grace, and having kept the Eucharistic fast are the basic conditions for receiving Communion worthily.
itens.corpo:
To receive Communion, one must first of all be a baptized Catholic and be in a state of grace, that is, without unconfessed mortal sin. The Code of Canon Law establishes, in canon 916, that anyone conscious of grave sin must not receive Communion without previously having made a sacramental confession, unless there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess — in which case the person must at least make an act of perfect contrition, with the resolution to go to confession as soon as possible.

Venial sin, unlike mortal sin, does not prevent Communion: on the contrary, the Eucharist itself is a remedy that strengthens the Christian against everyday weaknesses. Added to this are the observance of the brief Eucharistic fast of one hour before receiving Communion and an attitude of respect and reverence: these are simple requirements, but they help the child understand that the Eucharist is not ordinary food, and that approaching it calls for a prepared heart.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, can. 916
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1385, 1415

itens.resumo: The Mass does not repeat Christ's sacrifice on the cross: it makes present, in a sacramental way, the one sacrifice that He offered once for all.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in numbers 1367-1368, that the sacrifice of Christ on the cross and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice: the victim is one and the same, the same now offering through the ministry of priests who then offered himself on the cross — only the manner of offering differs, unbloody in the Mass and bloody on Calvary. The Eucharist is, therefore, the memorial of Christ's Passover: and in the biblical sense, a memorial is not merely the remembrance of something past, but the proclamation and sacramental actualization of that unique event.

The Eucharist is also, according to number 1368, the sacrifice of the Church herself: as the body of Christ, she participates in the offering of her Head, uniting to Christ's offering the prayers, joys, and sufferings of each of the faithful present at the celebration. Understanding this sacrificial dimension — and not only the communal or sharing aspect — helps the child understand why the Mass is called the "Holy Sacrifice," and not merely a meal or a prayer gathering.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1367-1368

itens.resumo: Communion given to those who are about to leave this life, "provision for the journey" that accompanies the Christian in the passage to the Father.
itens.corpo:
Viaticum comes from the Latin viaticum (from via, "road") and means "provision for the journey." In the tradition of the Church, it is the name given to the Eucharist received by those in danger of death: besides the Anointing of the Sick, the Church offers to those who are about to leave this life the very Body of Christ, received at this moment of passage with a very particular meaning and importance.

The Catechism, in nos. 1524-1525, teaches that Penance, the Anointing of the Sick, and the Eucharist as viaticum constitute, at the end of the Christian's earthly pilgrimage, "the sacraments that prepare for entering the heavenly homeland." Teaching this reality to the child who is preparing for First Communion helps to place the gift received within a larger horizon: the same Eucharist that the child will receive for the first time will continue to accompany him or her — God willing, many times throughout life — until the last moment, as food for the final journey to the Father's house.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1524-1525

itens.resumo: A feast instituted in 1264 that publicly celebrates, with a procession through the streets, the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
itens.corpo:
The feast of Corpus Christi ("Body of Christ") was born in the thirteenth century in Liège, in present-day Belgium, linked to the insistence of Saint Juliana of Cornillon (or of Liège), an Augustinian religious who, according to tradition, had a symbolic vision asking the Church to institute a feast of its own in honor of the Most Blessed Sacrament. In 1264, Pope Urban IV officially instituted the solemnity for the whole Church by the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo.

The celebration became known above all for its procession: it is the only day of the year on which, in many places, the Most Blessed Sacrament leaves the church and travels through the streets, exposed in a monstrance, accompanied by hymns and prayers of the faithful. Corpus Christi processions, encouraged by indulgences granted by popes such as Martin V and Eugene IV, became particularly common from the fourteenth century onward and remain, to this day, among the most visible and popular expressions of Catholic Eucharistic faith.
fontes: Urban IV, Bull Transiturus de hoc mundo (1264)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1378

itens.titulo: The Bread of Life in the Gospel of John
itens.resumo: In chapter 6 of the Gospel of John, Jesus announces, even before the Last Supper, that his body will be true food for eternal life.
itens.corpo:
Chapter 6 of the Gospel of John is one of the most important biblical passages for understanding the Eucharist. It begins with the multiplication of the loaves and fishes, when Jesus, starting from five loaves and two fish, feeds a multitude — a sign that anticipates, in a symbolic way, the spiritual gift He would later institute at the Last Supper. Soon afterward, beginning at verse 22, Jesus delivers in Capernaum the long discourse known as the "Bread of Life discourse."

In this discourse, Jesus explains that the manna that fed the Israelites in the desert, in the time of Moses, was only a figure of a superior food that the Father wanted to offer, and he states clearly: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven [...] and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world" (Jn 6:51). The child preparing for First Communion can find in this chapter, read slowly and calmly, the very words of Jesus announcing, even before the Last Supper, the gift that the child is about to receive for the first time.
fontes: Gospel of John 6:1-71
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1338

itens.titulo: Prefigurations of the Eucharist in the Old Testament
itens.resumo: The bread and wine of Melchizedek, the manna in the desert, and the Passover lamb prepare, in the Old Testament, the gift that Jesus would institute at the Last Supper.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in number 1333, that the Church recognizes in the gesture of the priest-king Melchizedek, who "brought out bread and wine" to bless Abraham (Gen 14:18-20), a prefiguration of the Eucharistic offering itself. Another important sign is the manna: the "bread from heaven" that fed the people of Israel for forty years in the desert (Ex 16:14-15) — Jesus himself, in the Bread of Life discourse, compares himself to this food, but states that he gives something greater, capable of granting eternal life (Jn 6:31-33).

A third sign is the Passover lamb: in the account of Exodus, it was to be sacrificed and its flesh entirely eaten by the family in memory of the liberation from Egypt (Ex 12:1-14), a rite repeated every year by the Jewish people. Saint Paul interprets this lamb as a figure of Christ, writing to the Christians of Corinth that "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7). Knowing these three prefigurations helps the child to realize that the Eucharist did not appear suddenly at the Last Supper, but was long prepared throughout the whole history of salvation narrated in the Old Testament.
fontes: Genesis 14:18-20
1 Corinthians 5:7
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1333

itens.resumo: Alongside the family, the catechist accompanies and helps the child to know and love Jesus Christ during preparation for First Communion.
itens.corpo:
Although parents remain the first of those responsible for the education of their children in the faith, the formal catechesis preparing for First Communion is normally conducted by catechists — for the most part lay people who voluntarily dedicate themselves to this service in the parish. The General Directory for Catechesis teaches that the formation of the catechist must prepare him, above all, to be himself a faithful, humble and joyful disciple, capable of communicating not only content, but a living experience of faith.

Besides knowing well the Christian message he is to transmit, a good catechist needs to know how to relate to children and to adapt language and methods to the age and circumstances of each class, building an itinerary that helps the little catechumen to identify, little by little, with Jesus Christ. The Directory considers the formation of catechists of deep faith a priority task of the Church, precisely because the quality of the sacramental preparation offered to children depends in great part on them.
fontes: Congregation for the Clergy, General Directory for Catechesis (1997)

itens.resumo: When receiving the host, the faithful respond "Amen" to the statement "The Body of Christ" — a small word that expresses faith in the real presence.
itens.corpo:
In the rite of Communion, described in the General Instruction of the Roman Missal, the priest or minister presents the consecrated host to each of the faithful, saying "The Body of Christ," and the one about to receive Communion responds "Amen" before receiving it. This Hebrew word, which means something like "so be it" or "it is true," is the same one used at the end of prayers and of the Creed, and here it serves as a small but decisive personal profession of faith.

By saying "Amen" at that moment, the faithful person is not merely following a script of words: they are affirming, with their own voice, that they believe that what they are about to receive is not ordinary bread, but truly the Body of Christ. Teaching the child the weight of this simple word — said in a clear voice, without hurry, looking at the host — helps keep Communion from becoming a mechanical gesture, and makes conscious, each time, the act of faith that Communion always requires.
tags: General Instruction of the Roman Missal
fontes: General Instruction of the Roman Missal, no. 161

itens.resumo: In some parishes, the child brings to the celebration a candle lit from the Paschal Candle, recalling the gesture made on the day of their Baptism.
itens.corpo:
The Paschal Candle — the large white candle blessed at the Easter Vigil, a symbol of the risen Christ, "light that conquers the darkness" — remains lit beside the baptismal font throughout the Easter Season and is used in celebrations such as Baptism, Confirmation and, in some parishes, also First Communion. On the day of Baptism, it is from this candle that the candle given to the child's parents and godparents, on the child's behalf, is lit, as a sign that the child has received the light of Christ.

In some communities, the custom is kept of the child bringing to First Communion that same candle — or a new one, lit from the Paschal Candle —, visibly recalling the gesture of their own Baptism. Although the custom is not a universal liturgical requirement, it helps the family and the child to perceive the connection between the sacraments of Christian initiation: the light received at Baptism is the same light that now illuminates the path to the Eucharistic table.
fontes: Rite of Baptism for Children
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1243
